passage: During the Diwali cleaning, Pankaj found an old magazine under the sofa and flipped to the stars page. "Listen! 'You are kind, but sometimes shy with new people. You hide your worries behind a smile.'" He looked up, amazed. "That's exactly me. How did they know?" His sister Mridul, dusting the shelf, grabbed the magazine. "Let me read mine." She read the line for her sign and frowned. Then she read Pankaj's again. "That could be anyone. Even Papa is shy with new people sometimes." "No, it's me," Pankaj said, and tore the page out carefully to keep in his school bag.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj find the old magazine?
qa.a: Under the sofa.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he read his horoscope?
qa.a: He felt amazed and understood, sure the line described him exactly.

qa.q: What could Pankaj try to test whether the horoscope is really about him?
qa.a: He could read the lines for other signs and see whether they fit him too, or ask family whether his line fits them.

qa.q: How does Mridul see the horoscope line?
qa.a: Mridul sees it as so general that it could describe anyone, even Papa.

grounding: Illustrates a child sure a general horoscope line describes him exactly, not noticing it fits almost anyone.

subtype: Online quiz result feels like being seen [Actor]
passage: "Saurabh, come here! I did the personality quiz." It was the first week of the summer holidays, and Lavanya was lying on the floor under the fan with her phone. "What did it say?" "'You are a deep thinker who feels things more than others realise. People see your strength but not your sensitivity.'" She clutched the phone to her chest. "That's literally me." "Let me try." Saurabh tapped through the questions. "Mine says, 'You have hidden depths others don't always see.'" "That's different." "Is it?" Lavanya ignored him and shared hers to her status. "Finally, something that gets me." Three friends replied within minutes: "SAME!!" Lavanya didn't notice what that meant.

qa.q: Where was Lavanya lying while doing the quiz?
qa.a: On the floor under the fan.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya clutch the phone to her chest?
qa.a: She felt deeply understood and moved, wanting to believe the quiz really saw who she is.

qa.q: What might help Lavanya see how general the result is?
qa.a: Comparing her result with Saurabh's and noticing that three friends said "SAME!!" to the exact same words.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see the quiz results?
qa.a: Saurabh is sceptical, noticing that his result sounds almost the same as Lavanya's.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling understood by a flattering, general quiz result and sharing it as proof of who she is.

subtype: Reading or prediction that seems to know them [Receiver]
passage: The Navratri fair was half washed out by rain, and Himani had only a little money left after her bus fare. Still, she stopped at the tarot reader's tent with Jagdish, mostly to get out of the drizzle. The reader turned a card and looked at her kindly. "You carry an old hurt you rarely mention." Himani's throat tightened. How could she know? The reader went on, warmly, and Himani found herself nodding at everything. "And the move to a new city you're thinking about. The cards say wait." Himani had been planning to accept the Pune college seat. On the bus home, she said, "Maybe I shouldn't go." Jagdish frowned. "Himani, everybody has an old hurt. She said that to the man before you too."

qa.q: Which college seat had Himani been planning to accept?
qa.a: The Pune college seat.

qa.q: Why did Himani's throat tighten at the reader's words?
qa.a: She felt seen and moved, as if the reader knew a private hurt, which made her trust the reader.

qa.q: What would you advise Himani before changing her plans?
qa.a: To remember the line fits most people, and to decide about Pune using real facts and people she trusts, not a card.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see the reading?
qa.a: Jagdish sees it as a general line said to everyone and worries it is steering Himani's choice.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult moved by a general line that seems to know her and how that warmth starts to steer a choice.

passage: Gargi had to reply to the job offer by six, and the palmist at the corner was her cousin Preeti's idea. "Just for fun. It's on the way." The old man studied her hand. "You are ambitious, but you also want peace. Sometimes you doubt yourself." Preeti gasped. Gargi smiled. "Would the opposite fit too? If you said I don't care about peace?" He laughed. "No, no." "Hmm. Anything specific? A date? A name?" He mentioned "a change near water." "We live in Mumbai," Gargi said. On the auto ride, with twenty minutes to spare, she opened her own list: salary, commute, team, what she'd learn. "The palm reading was nice. Made me think about wanting peace." She typed her reply. "But the list decides."

qa.q: By what time did Gargi have to reply to the job offer?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: How did Gargi seem to feel during the reading?
qa.a: She seemed amused and relaxed, enjoying it but staying sceptical enough to test the vague lines.

qa.q: What questions did Gargi use to test the palmist's statements?
qa.a: She asked whether the opposite would fit too and whether he could say anything specific and checkable.

qa.q: How does Preeti react to the reading?
qa.a: Preeti is impressed, gasping at the first line, while Gargi stays calm.

grounding: Shows a young professional testing vague palm-reading lines and enjoying the reflection without letting it decide her job.

subtype: Loves the lopsided thing they made [Actor]
passage: The winter clay class at the community centre smelled of wet mud. Lakshmi pressed and pinched until her pot stood up, lopsided, with a thumbprint on the side. "Mine!" Aunty put a shiny shop pot beside it for the paints. "Which one do you want to paint?" "Mine!" "But this one is so neat." Lakshmi hugged her wobbly pot. "Mine is the best. I made it." Samir, beside her, pointed at the shop pot. "Can I have that one?" "Yes," said Lakshmi, not even looking.

qa.q: What was on the side of Lakshmi's pot?
qa.a: A thumbprint.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi hug her wobbly pot?
qa.a: She felt proud and fond of it because she made it herself, so it felt more special than the neat one.

qa.q: How could Aunty respond to Lakshmi's choice?
qa.a: Aunty could let her paint her own pot and praise the effort she put into making it.

qa.q: How does Samir see the shop pot?
qa.a: Samir likes the neat shop pot and is happy to take it, since he has no special feeling for either.

grounding: Illustrates a young child treasuring the lopsided pot she made over a neat shop-bought one.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: Class 6 note, Christmas science fair week. Francis has spent four days on his volcano model with Lalit. When I pointed out that the tube was too narrow for the baking soda to foam out, Francis folded his arms. "It's fine. We tested it." (They hadn't.) I suggested a wider bottle. "No, then we'd have to start again." His voice shook a little. Lalit whispered, "Maybe Ma'am's right," and Francis glared at him. I could see the criticism felt personal after all those hours. What I did next: I praised the painted lava first, then asked them to test once, together, in front of me. The foam stuck in the tube. Francis stared. "Okay," he said quietly. "A wider bottle."

qa.q: How many days had Francis spent on the volcano model?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: Why did Francis's voice shake when the note-writer suggested a wider bottle?
qa.a: He felt defensive and hurt, as if criticism of the model after four days of effort were criticism of him.

qa.q: What helped Francis accept the change?
qa.a: Praising the painted lava first and then testing it together, so he could see the problem himself.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel when Francis glares at him?
qa.a: Lalit likely feels awkward and a little hurt, caught between his partner and the teacher.

grounding: Shows a child who resists suggestions on a model he built for days, feeling criticism as personal.

passage:
Subject: The date parser

Hi Joseph,

I've been thinking about Tuesday's review. I know you wrote the date parser yourself over two weekends, and it's clever work. I can see how much of you is in it. But when I suggested switching to the standard library, you said, "Ours is better," and I'm not sure the tests agree. It failed on leap years and on two regional formats. The library handles both. I don't think you're defending the code because it's better; I think you're defending it because you built it. I'd feel the same. Could we run both on the test set on Friday and let the results decide? Either way, those weekends taught you things the library never will.

Sachin

qa.q: How long did Joseph spend writing the date parser?
qa.a: Two weekends.

qa.q: What seems to be on Sachin's mind while writing this email?
qa.a: Sachin seems concerned but kind, noticing that the attachment comes from effort rather than quality, and careful not to hurt.

qa.q: What plan does Sachin propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Running both on the test set on Friday, so the results decide instead of pride or authority.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel reading the email?
qa.a: Joseph might feel a little defensive at first, but also respected, because the email honours the work.

grounding: Illustrates a team lead noticing a developer clinging to a self-built module for the effort spent rather than its quality.

passage: Before: On a Saturday, Seema stood in her flat looking at the bookshelf she had built herself last year, sanding every plank. It leaned. The books slid. Baljeet said, "Want to buy a proper one?" "Never!" she said. During: The next weekend, a shelf gave way and her books fell. Seema sat on the floor and asked herself honestly: if I were starting today, would I choose this shelf for my books? No. She felt a pang. After: Two weeks later, the books sat on a sturdy new shelf. Her handmade one stood by the window, holding only her plants and a photo. "Still my favourite," she told Baljeet. "Just not for heavy things."

qa.q: What did Seema sand when building the bookshelf?
qa.a: Every plank.

qa.q: What did Seema feel when she admitted she wouldn't choose the shelf today?
qa.a: She felt a pang of sadness, letting go of her pride in the labour to see the result honestly.

qa.q: How did Seema honour her effort without overrating it?
qa.a: She moved her books to a sturdy shelf but kept the handmade one by the window for plants and a photo.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Seema's final choice?
qa.a: Baljeet probably sees it as sensible and sweet: the books are safe, and the shelf she loves still has a place.

grounding: Shows an adult asking whether she would choose her handmade shelf today, while still cherishing it.

passage: During Holi week, the school library had a giant jigsaw of a tiger on the back table. Vinita was nearly done with the stripes when the bell rang for the colour-play assembly. "Come on!" Varun called. She went, but through all the gulal and music, she kept thinking about the empty corner by the tiger's ear. Where did that last curved piece go? She even dreamt of it. The spelling test she'd finished that morning? She couldn't remember a single word from it. The next day, she ran to the library before first bell, still with pink hands, and found the piece under the table. Snap. Done. By lunchtime, she'd forgotten all about the tiger.

qa.q: What picture was on the giant jigsaw?
qa.a: A tiger.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling during the assembly?
qa.a: She felt restless and distracted, her mind nagged by the unfinished corner of the puzzle.

qa.q: What could Vinita do next time she's called away from something unfinished?
qa.a: She could jot down where she stopped, so the open task nags less until she can return.

qa.q: How might Varun see Vinita at the assembly?
qa.a: Varun might find her distracted and puzzling, since she seems to be somewhere else during the fun.

grounding: Illustrates a child who cannot stop thinking about an unfinished puzzle but forgets finished tasks.

passage: Warden's note, Diwali break, boys' hostel. Most students have gone home; Abhinav stayed because of his exams. On Monday night I found him awake at two, watching a series on his laptop. "Just one more, sir. The last episode ended with the brother at the door with a gun, and I have to know." His roommate Imran said Abhinav had promised him three times to stop. The next evening I asked Abhinav how he felt when he tried to shut the laptop. "Irritated. Like my head won't let it go." What I did next: we agreed he would stop midway through an episode, not at the end, and leave the laptop in the common room at midnight. He said it felt strange but easier.

qa.q: What time did the warden find Abhinav awake?
qa.a: At two.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel when he tried to shut the laptop?
qa.a: He felt irritated and unsettled, as if his mind couldn't let go of the unresolved cliffhanger.

qa.q: Why might stopping midway through an episode help?
qa.a: It avoids ending on a fresh cliffhanger, so the open loop pulls less, and leaving the laptop out of the room removes the temptation.

qa.q: How might Imran feel about Abhinav's promises?
qa.a: Imran is probably frustrated and tired, having heard Abhinav promise three times to stop.

grounding: Shows a teenager unable to stop after a cliffhanger because the open loop keeps his mind engaged.
